chunks: "Shoot-through, or crowbar current, is when both the PMOS and NMOS in a CMOS stage are on at the same time, so current flows straight from V DD to ground instead of into the load.
It happens on every transition. The NMOS turns on once the input passes V tn , but the PMOS doesn't turn off until the input gets within V tp of V DD .
Between those, both are conducting, and the current peaks around the switching threshold, near V DD over 2 . On a normal fast edge that's a short spike and a modest power cost.
It gets bad when the input edge is slow, or when an input is left floating and sits near mid-rail, because then the crowbar current flows for a long time or continuously.

To prevent it in logic: keep input edges fast, use Schmitt-trigger inputs for slow or noisy signals so the internal edge is fast, never leave CMOS inputs floating, and size stages so input and output transition times are similar.
For output drivers and power stages, where the two FETs can have separate gate signals, you use break-before-make: turn the PMOS fully off, wait a dead time, then turn the NMOS on, and vice versa.
That's exactly what half-bridge gate drivers do, because there a shoot-through event can short the supply through two power FETs and destroy them."
